title: Choking, infant
summary: Baby under 1 year who cannot cough, cry or breathe: 5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts, repeated. Never abdominal thrusts.

steps.text: Can the baby cough forcefully or cry?
steps.detail:
This protocol is for babies younger than about 1 year. For older children and adults use Choking, adult and child.

Signs of a severe blockage: the baby cannot cough or cry, has a weak cough, or cannot breathe.

If the baby is coughing strongly or crying, air is moving. Let them cough and watch closely.

ask.q: Is the baby coughing forcefully or crying?

steps.text: Let the baby keep coughing. Stay with them and watch closely.
steps.detail:
Do not give back blows or chest thrusts while the baby is coughing strongly or crying.

If the cough becomes weak or silent, or the baby cannot cry or breathe, start back blows and chest thrusts.

ask.q: Has the cough become weak or silent, or can the baby no longer cry or breathe?

steps.text: Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty. Start helping right away.
steps.detail: A baby with a severe blockage can stop breathing quickly. Start back blows straight away and have someone else go for help.

steps.text: Lay the baby face down along your forearm, resting on your thigh, head lower than the chest. Support the jaw with your fingers.
steps.detail: Sit, kneel or stand. Hold the baby's jaw between your thumb and fingers to support the head. Turn the baby face down along your forearm, and rest your forearm on your thigh for support. Keep the head lower than the body.

steps.text: Give 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
steps.detail: Use the heel of your free hand. Strike firmly between the shoulder blades, up to 5 times.

steps.text: Turn the baby face up on your other forearm, head lower than the chest. Give 5 quick chest thrusts with the heel of one hand on the centre of the chest.
steps.detail:
Support the back of the baby's head with your hand and turn the baby over so they lie face up along your other forearm, resting on your thigh. Keep the head lower than the chest.

Place the heel of one hand on the centre of the chest, on the lower half of the breastbone just below the nipple line. Give 5 quick, firm thrusts straight down, about 1.5 inches deep.

Current guidance (AHA 2025) uses the heel of one hand for infant chest thrusts because it pushes deeper than the older two-finger method. Some lay materials still show two fingers; the heel of one hand is the current recommendation.

Chest thrusts are not the same as CPR compressions: they are separate, forceful pushes to dislodge the object, not a steady rhythm.

ask.q: Is the object out, or is the baby coughing, crying or breathing again?

steps.text: Not cleared? Keep repeating 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts until it comes out or the baby becomes unresponsive.
steps.detail: Keep alternating: turn face down for 5 back blows, then face up for 5 chest thrusts.

ask.q: Is the baby still responsive (awake, moving)?

steps.text: The baby is unresponsive: lay them on a firm, flat surface and start infant CPR, beginning with chest compressions.
steps.detail:
Use the CPR, infant protocol. Start with compressions; do not check for a pulse.

Each time you open the airway to give breaths, look in the mouth. If you can see the object, take it out. Never sweep a finger blindly in the baby's mouth.

If help has not been called yet: call 911 if you have signal; if not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty.

steps.text: Cleared. Hold the baby, keep them calm, and watch their breathing.
steps.detail:
Keep watching breathing and alertness. If the blockage seems to return, start this protocol again.

Any baby who needed back blows and chest thrusts should be checked by a medical professional.

steps.text: Keep watching until the baby is breathing easily.
steps.detail: If at any point the cough becomes weak or silent, or the baby cannot cry or breathe, start this protocol again.

donts: Do not give abdominal thrusts to a baby under 1 year; they can injure the organs in the belly.
Do not do blind finger sweeps in the baby's mouth; only remove an object you can see.
Do not give back blows or chest thrusts to a baby who is coughing strongly or crying.
evacuate: Evacuate urgently a baby who became unresponsive or needed CPR.
Get medical evaluation for any baby who needed back blows and chest thrusts.
